p: Two Tuesdays went by without Kit bringing Vern her one sentence. He asked once, and then he let it be.

On the March drill her assistant crew chief, Fisk, came in off a night at the warehouse, and Kit gave him a wheel change on two two eight anyway. The forms said the wheel was torqued, with his initials. At the tool crib she found the torque wrench had never left its hook.

She held the jet first and wrote it up. Then she walked Fisk to the far side of the jet, where nobody could hear, and they torqued the wheel together. He owned the radio call too, the one where he'd said the forms were done. He hadn't told her he was worn out, he said, because she'd have pulled him, and then she'd know.

She took him straight to Boyd and let him tell it himself. Boyd took him off torque tasks until Kit retrains him and sent it up the line in writing. When Boyd asked about Fisk's night shift, Kit said she'd seen it at four and let it go. Boyd said that was how he'd want the shop run when he's gone.

That afternoon Kit read one of Vern's old logs, the first one where he'd written MY MISS. She thought about her own 2019 score sheet, folded under the foam in her toolbox, and how she'd always said it was Boyd's.

She got her test voucher at the base test office, in the building where she'd sat the test in 2019, and said no to the room at the end of the hall. That night she told Graham the whole day, her own part included, and booked the test herself: Saturday, May 15, at eight in the morning, in Kansas City. She wiped the question mark off Graham's whiteboard, and in the morning he texted that he'd drive.

On Sunday she gave the safety brief as her own miss and left Fisk's name out of it. In the heritage room Vern ran her through a timed analogy block in test order. Down the margin she'd written thirty eight minutes for reading, the old paper test's number. She guessed the last three, and her hands were flat on the table. Vern told her she'd sat it before.
Leon Yates. The night lead at the Tolliver water plant, sixty one.
Patrice Pruett. Vern's wife of fifty one years, a retired librarian.

She did Vern's twenty five word problems in twenty seven of the twenty nine minutes, and he marked them with his pencil while she sat across from him with her coat still on. Nineteen right. He wrote the number at the top of the first page and went through the six she'd missed one at a time, slow, as if nothing else had been said in that room all afternoon. Two were rates where she'd mixed up minutes and hours. He circled those twice.
At five he locked the heritage room. Out in the lot he said Tuesday, and she said Tuesday.

Then she drove back across the ramp to the shop, which was dark except for the light over the coffee, and opened her toolbox. She lifted the shadow board foam out by one corner, the way you'd lift a floor mat looking for a spare key. The papers were where they'd been for seven years, soft at the creases. She took the top one and put the foam back down over the rest. Then she buttoned the sheet into the inside pocket of her coat and drove to the plant for an eleven o'clock shift.

Monday, March 8, twenty to three in the morning, and the residual alarm went off. At the Tolliver plant that's a two note beep and a yellow box on the screen that says LOW RESIDUAL CLEARWELL. No horn. Nobody'd hear it from the lot, and at that hour nobody's in the lot. Yates, the night lead, was down at the river intake with a flashlight, cussing at the screen down there for packing up with leaves again. He did that most nights in March.
Point nine nine leaving the plant. They liked it around one four, and the alarm was set at one even. She got up, and the sheet in her coat crackled, and she let it.

Chemical room, end of the hall. The hypo pump's a gray plastic box on the wall about the size of a lunch pail, over a drum of the stuff. Hypochlorite. Call it bleach if you want, it's just a lot meaner than what's under your sink. The pump was clicking along like it was any other night. Click, green light, click, green light. The clear tube from the drum up to it was full of little bubbles, though, all the way up. And the line out the other side, the one to the injection point, wasn't going anywhere.

Bucket from under the sink. She held it under the priming valve on the pump head and cracked the valve a quarter turn, and it spat at her, foam and a burp of gas and then yellow. The clicking got heavy. You could hear it. She shut the valve. Boyd always said don't walk off from a thing the second it starts working, so she gave it another minute, standing there at three in the morning with a bucket of bleach foam, till the line was yellow all the way to the wall.

I learned this one in Guam, standing behind a crew chief who was bleeding a brake line at three in the morning. He called every bubble by name, and none of the names would go in a log. "Air squashes," he told me. "Fluid don't. That's the whole lesson." Your pump's got the same disease. Bleach is always coming apart a little and gassing off, the gas rides up into the pump head, and then the pump's squeezing a bubble all night and calling it work.

Back at the console she pulled up the night's readings, every half hour since midnight, the way the plant printed them for the log. What she was after was the last good number before the drop. That'd tell her how long the town's water had gone out light.

Readings every half hour from midnight to three. Plant flow, in million gallons a day: one point two six, one point two five, one point two five, one point two four, one point two five, one point two five, one point two six. Chlorine residual, in milligrams per liter: one point four two, one point four one, one point four oh, one point three eight, one point two one, one point oh six, point nine four. Feed pump, percent: forty eight at every reading.

Finger on 0130, finger on the residual row: 1.38. Then the neighbors, so she'd know what a slip would have looked like. 1.40 before it, 1.21 after, and 1.24 up in the flow row. So the pump had quit a little after half past one, and the water had gone out light for the better part of two hours. The bottom row said 48 percent all night. The pump had reported what it was told to do, not what it did.

Row, then column, then a look around the cell. On the test many of the wrong choices sit right next to the answer. And notice that bottom row. The pump said forty eight all night long. A gauge that shows you the setting isn't showing you the flow. I've been lied to by better instruments than that one.

The log had a line for chlorine fed, in pounds a day, and the night's was hers to fill in. March's dose was 2.4 milligrams per liter; Gene had set it on the first. The plant was making 1.25 million gallons a day.

Everybody at the plant knew the pounds formula the way they knew the gate code. Milligrams per liter, times million gallons a day, times 8.34, which is what a gallon of water weighs. Every line above hers in the log said 25.0, the same number night after night in four different handwritings. She worked it anyway, on the back of the clipboard. A number somebody else wrote down was somebody else's arithmetic.

2.4 times 1.25 is 3, the friendly kind of number. Three times 8.34 is 25.02. She wrote 25.0 on the line like everybody else. Then in the remarks she started on the rest: what the pump had actually done between half past one and a quarter after three, which wasn't 25 of anything.

Strength, times flow, times what a gallon weighs. The 8.34 is what turns milligrams per liter and millions of gallons into pounds you could lift. Every wrong choice here is that formula with one piece dropped or a decimal slid, which is how a lot of wrong choices get built. Round it first. Two and a half times one and a quarter is about three, three eights is twenty four, so the answer lives near twenty five.

Yates came back up from the intake at half past three with river mud on his boots and wet leaves stuck to the knees of his coveralls. He was sixty one and had worked nights at the plant since before Kit could drive. He read the screen over her shoulder, then the remarks she'd started, and pulled out the other chair.

Leave that out. She asked him why. It came back. Never got anywhere near the floor. He rubbed his eyes with the heels of his hands. And it's the third time this month. I primed it twice on my nights and kept it out of the book. You write tonight's, and Gene reads it at the huddle and asks why it's the first one.
He didn't say it mean. He said it like a man reading a gauge he didn't care for, and then he sat and waited to see what she'd do with the pen.

I'm writing tonight's, Leon. All of it. He looked at the pen a while. She told him the other two nights weren't hers. She hadn't seen them, and she wasn't going to write them for him. They go in the book before Gene reads it at seven. If they're not there, I'll tell him I knew. Yates said she was a pain in the neck, and there wasn't much behind it. At twenty to seven he sat down at the far end of the desk and wrote two short lines under hers, with dates, and went home without saying good night, which for Yates was about normal.

Integrity, with a lead who runs that desk. Your own record you write true, whoever asks you not to. His nights are his to write, and you tell him so to his face with a time on it, before you'd carry them anywhere else. You didn't go over his head at half past three, and you didn't sign up to keep it for him. What would that book have said the night nobody caught it?

On Tuesday she slept till two, and at seven she was on Cedar Street at the brick ranch with the dead hedge. The porch light was on. Down the hall the television was going, low, the way it always was. On the drive over she'd thought about Yates in the chair beside hers at half past three, asking her to leave one night out of the book. She'd been leaving one out for seven years.

Vern had the reading book open to where they'd stopped and the egg timer beside it. She didn't sit. She took the sheet out of her coat and unfolded it on the yellow table and pressed the creases flat with the side of her hand, and he let her do all of that without a word.
Air Force Officer Qualifying Test. Test date, nineteen October, twenty nineteen. Pilot, nineteen. CSO, forty four. Verbal, seventy one. Quantitative, thirty eight. Academic Aptitude, fifty five.

Pilot came back nineteen. You need twenty five. She said the rest standing up, with her coat still on. Boyd asked me to stay for the inspection that winter. He really asked. I said yes because yes was easier than saying nineteen out loud. She kept her eyes on the sheet. Then I let the shop have it. My mother. Graham. Boyd worst of all. He's spent seven years thinking he cost me something, and I let him. Vern read the sheet top to bottom, every line. Then he put one finger under PILOT. Instrument Comprehension? Ran out of time. I guessed the last nine. He nodded like that was a number he could use, and pointed at the other chair, and she sat.

He didn't say anything about the sheet. He got up and poured two coffees from the percolator, though she hadn't asked for one, and sat back down and turned his class ring on his finger, the one worn thin on one side. She'd seen him do it at the diner without knowing she'd noticed.

Spring of seventy three. You know about the gym. I bought this ring the winter before, and wore it to the flight physical so I'd have something to turn. He turned it. Eye chart on the back of a door. I read it right down to the line that counted, and that line came out like somebody'd breathed on it. One line. The flight surgeon wrote one word on my form, and that night I went and looked it up, like the dictionary might've had it wrong.

He took a pencil out of the coffee can and printed it in the margin of her sheet, under her 19, in his capitals. ACUITY. It was the first word anybody had ever written on that page. Closest in meaning, Sergeant.

Sharpness. Sharpness. I had all of it but one line. The navigator school had offered him a seat the same week, he said, and he'd said yes before the man finished asking. He left the word where it was, in the margin under her 19, and she let it stay.

So I navigated. Tolliver's tankers till they pulled the seat, and from eighty five on, the rest of the month, I dispatched for a freight outfit in Kansas City. He drank some coffee. Did my dispatcher course in eighty five with a kid from Denver named Walt Herrera, twenty three, best weather head in the room. Thirty one years after that I signed releases for airplanes I never got on. My name went next to the captain's on every one of them.

Kit had the card in her coat too. She'd written it Monday at four in the morning, after the pump came back, in pen on an index card out of the supply drawer at the plant. She took it out and set it face up by his coffee. I WANT TO FLY. It was the sentence from LETTER 2, the one she'd never printed.
Vern read it once. He stood it up against the percolator, where it would be in front of him every time he poured, and went down the hall to the den. He came back with a log out of the box.

My log, twenty seven February, oh one. Tolliver, preflight. Crew chief found fuel weeping at a panel under the left wing. Oh five twenty, counted twelve drops in four minutes. Oh five fifty, counted fifteen drops in three minutes. Crew chief wrote it up. No go. I had the fuel to fly it. Not the question.
She didn't ask whose jet it was.

Twelve in four minutes is three a minute. Fifteen in three is five. Two a minute faster in half an hour, and still climbing when they quit counting. She looked at his last line a long time. I had the fuel to fly it. Not the question. For seven years she'd let a nineteen answer whether she should fly. Nobody had asked her whether she wanted to. Crew chief was right, Vern said, and that was all he said about that.

Graham was at the kitchen table on Orchard Street with a stack of lab reports and a red pen when she got home at half past nine. He'd left the porch light on and the radio off. Behind him on the fridge he'd boxed off Saturday, April 3, in green: PRACTICE TEST, 5 HRS, ME ON THE CLOCK.
On Saturday she'd told him all of the wheel, her own part in it too, standing at that counter. That had been hard. This one she'd been carrying a lot longer.

She hung her coat on the hook by the door with the sheet still in the inside pocket. He looked up from a sophomore's graph and took her in, the coat and the hook and her face. You look like he made you do long division for two hours straight. How was Vern tonight?

There's a part of 2019 you haven't heard. It's mine. It isn't Boyd's. Graham put the red pen down on the graph. Do you want to tell me now? Not tonight. Tonight it'd come out as Boyd's story with a different ending. Saturday the third, after the practice test. All of it, with the paper on the table. Okay. It came right away this time, no beat in front of it. Then she heard what she'd said. After the practice test. Nine years of afters, and she'd just handed him one more, and he'd taken it the way he took all the others. Before he went up to bed he took the marker off the fridge and wrote 2019 in the square for Saturday, April 3, small, in his own black.
At Monday's huddle Gene read all three lines, hers and Yates's two under it, and didn't make a speech about any of them. He ordered a valve before lunch.

Her next stretch of nights started at eleven Wednesday night. There was a note taped to the pump in Gene's square printing: DEGAS VALVE ORDERED. CHECK THE HEAD EVERY HOUR TILL IT COMES. At three Thursday morning she did the check.

Then she read the drum. At eleven, when she came on, the sight tube had said 50 gallons. Now it said 46. The plant changed drums at 10, never lower, because the bottom of a drum was where the worst of it settled. Day shift would want to know when to have the next one on the dolly.

Fifty to forty six in four hours is a gallon an hour, twenty four a day, same as the log said. Forty six less the ten she couldn't use is thirty six. Thirty six gallons at one an hour is thirty six hours, and three Thursday morning plus thirty six hours is three Friday afternoon. She wrote CHANGE DRUM FRI 1500 on the board by the door and put her initials after it.

Three steps, and each one feeds the next. Get the rate from the two readings, take off what you can't use, then divide and add it to the clock from where you're standing. Four gallons in four hours is one an hour. Thirty six above the line is thirty six hours. The step people skip is the floor, the ten gallons nobody's allowed to pull.
The next Tuesday the card was still standing against the percolator.

This one I can't teach you. He laid a typed page on the table. Twenty statements, each with a row of five boxes, strongly disagree on one end and strongly agree on the other. None of these came off the test. I wrote them at this table Sunday. The real one's two hundred forty in forty five minutes, and nobody grades it, and nobody can tell you what to put. Eleven seconds a line. He cranked the egg timer to four.

She went fast. I like to know the plan before I start. Moderately agree. I'd rather fix a thing myself than ask for help. Strongly agree. I stay calm when things go wrong. Moderately agree. Then number eleven. When I want something, I say so.
Her pencil was in the moderately agree box before she'd read to the end, the way your hand finds the light switch in your own kitchen. Then it stopped there.

She moved the pencil two boxes over and marked moderately disagree. It took about two seconds. For seven years she'd described herself as the crew chief who stayed, and she'd described her well, and it had been the wrong woman. She did the last nine fast. When the timer rang, Vern turned the page face down without reading a word of it. Those are yours.
After that he set the night's arithmetic, ten problems in his capitals, and she did them on the egg timer.

A receiver came onto the boom needing 21,000 pounds. For the first six minutes the boom passed fuel at 2,500 pounds a minute. Then the receiver's tanks started to fill, the flow slowed to 1,500 pounds a minute, and it stayed there to the end.
Underneath, in his capitals: HOW LONG ON THE BOOM. He'd underlined LONG.

Six minutes at twenty five hundred is fifteen thousand. That leaves six thousand at fifteen hundred a minute, four minutes more. Ten. She wrote it and circled it. Vern looked at the circle, then up at the stove clock. Nine already. He said that would do for one night.

When the rate changes partway, cut the problem where it changes and work each piece. Averaging two rates only works when each one ran the same length of time, and these didn't. Six minutes fast, four slow. Every boom operator I ever flew with said the last few thousand pounds take the longest, and none of them was ever wrong about it.

At the front door that night the television down the hall went quiet, and a small woman came out of there. Short white hair, reading glasses shoved up on her head, a pie in a glass dish under a dish towel.

You're the sergeant. I'm Patrice. It's gooseberry. I froze them in June, and he'll eat the whole thing standing up if it stays in this house. She put it in Kit's hands. Then she looked back toward the kitchen. Vern had the water running over the cups and was pretending he couldn't hear. He hasn't talked this much in years. He won't tell me what about, which is how I know it's yours. She tipped her head at the percolator. And that card's been against my coffee pot a week. He moves it to pour and puts it back.

On Saturday, March 20, Kit brought the dish back washed, to the heritage room, because she knew he'd be there. Nobody had wandered in. He had the reading book open on the cleared table, and he shoved the egg timer over so the dish had somewhere to go.
Graham had a date. It was on the whiteboard in his black marker, 2019 in the square for April 3, and she saw it every morning when she got the milk out.
She hadn't come about the dish.
Keep it till I've told Graham and Boyd myself. Graham first. Then ask me if I did. Vern let her get all the way to the end of it. I can ask.
Vern looked at the pie dish for a while. Patrice's dish, washed, with the dish towel folded on top of it the way Patrice had sent it.
It isn't mine to tell, Sergeant. He moved the dish an inch, for no reason. And it isn't yours to keep forever.

Then he dug in the corduroy jacket, the one from the diner in January, and came up with a log folded once. He gave her logs on Tuesdays, at the end of the night, picked for the week's work. This wasn't a Tuesday, and he didn't say what it was for. He held it out across the table anyway.
Kit took it and didn't open it. It rode home on the passenger seat, under her right hand at every stop sign on the river road.
